Smitten
smit'n
v. (past participle of smite: struck, afflicted; rendering Hebrew nakah, Greek patasso)
Past participle of smite, from the Saxon smitan, to strike. The Hebrew nakah covers everything from a blow of the hand to a plague sent from heaven, and its passive participle raises the question every sufferer asks — smitten by whom?

Biblical Definition

Smitten is the participle of being struck, and Scripture uses it above all of the Servant, where it exposes a fatal misreading and then corrects it. Isaiah writes: “Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted” (Isaiah 53:4). The onlookers were not wrong that he was smitten of God — the next verses say the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all — they were wrong about why. They assumed he was suffering for his own sin, as Job's friends assumed of Job, and that assumption is the oldest error in the theology of suffering. He was wounded for our transgressions, and the chastisement of our peace was upon him. The word also describes the believer's inner affliction with unusual honesty: “My heart is smitten, and withered like grass; so that I forget to eat my bread” (Psalm 102:4) — a description of grief so heavy that appetite fails, preserved in the Psalter as a prayer rather than edited out. Scripture does not present the life of faith as immune from being smitten, and it locates the meaning of the blow in God's hand rather than in the sufferer's guilt.

Webster 1828 Definition

Past participle of smite — struck, afflicted. Isaiah's Servant was smitten of God, but for our transgressions and not his own; and the Psalter records hearts smitten and withered like grass.

expand to see more

SMITTEN, pp. of smite. [Sax. smitan, to strike.] Struck; beaten; killed.

2. Afflicted; visited with judgment or with disease; as, smitten with a plague.

3. Affected with strong feeling; as, the heart is smitten.

4. Blasted; withered; as, the corn was smitten with blasting, Amos 4.

5. In Scripture, of the Servant; as, we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted, Isa. 53.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 53:4 — "Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted."

Psalm 102:4 — "My heart is smitten, and withered like grass; so that I forget to eat my bread."

Psalm 44:22 — "Yea, for thy sake are we killed all the day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter."

Luke 19:41 — "And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it,"

Modern Corruption

Suffering is read as a verdict on the sufferer — the oldest error, and the one Job's friends made. Isaiah 53 shows the perfectly innocent One smitten of God, which severs the link between affliction and personal guilt.

expand to see more

The retribution reflex is universal and persistent: the sick man must have sinned, the bankrupt must have been foolish, the bereaved must have lacked faith. The disciples brought it to Christ at the man born blind — who did sin, this man, or his parents? — and he answered that neither had. Isaiah 53:4 records the same reflex operating at Calvary, where onlookers esteemed the Servant smitten of God and drew the obvious conclusion about his character. They were watching the atonement and reading it as a judgment on the victim's own record.

There is a modern variant in prosperity teaching, which simply runs the logic forwards: if the righteous are not smitten, then a man who is smitten must be deficient in faith or in giving. It is Job's comforters with a microphone, and it leaves the afflicted believer doubly burdened. The principle to recover is that Scripture assigns affliction to God's hand without assigning it to the sufferer's guilt. Psalm 102:4 prays honestly out of a smitten heart, and Isaiah 53 shows the only man who never deserved a blow taking every blow that we did.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nakah is to strike, from a slap to a plague, and its passive participle is the word in Isaiah 53:4; maggephah is a stroke or plague. Greek patasso is to strike, used in I will smite the shepherd.

expand to see more

Hebrew nakah (H5221) — to smite, to strike, to afflict; used of blows, of plagues, and of the Servant.

Hebrew maggephah (H4046) — a stroke, a plague; the smiting sent among Israel.

Hebrew chalah (H2470) — to be weak or sick; the condition of one smitten with disease.

Greek patasso (G3960) — to strike, to smite; I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.

Greek mastigoo (G3146) — to scourge; whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son.

Usage

"Of the Servant misread by onlookers: we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted (Isaiah 53:4)."

"Of grief that takes away appetite: my heart is smitten, and withered like grass (Psalm 102:4)."

"Of a nation under judgment, as when Israel was smitten before her enemies for sin in the camp."
